Sensualism
In
epistemology
,
sensualism
(also
sensationalism
or
sensationism
) is a doctrine whereby
sensations
and
perception
are the basic and most important form of true
cognition
. It may oppose abstract ideas.
[
1
]
This question was long ago put forward in
Greek philosophy
(
Stoicism
,
Epicureanism
) and further developed to the full by the British and French Sensualists (
John Locke
,
David Hume
,
Étienne Bonnot de Condillac
) and the
British Associationists
(
Thomas Brown
,
David Hartley
,
Joseph Priestley
). In the 19th century, it was very much taken up by the
Positivists
(
Auguste Comte
,
Herbert Spencer
,
Hippolyte Taine
,
Émile Littré
).
